item.title: CAS review: Sebi announces last 30-minute VWAP method for settlement
item.description: Sebi has revised the closing auction session framework, adopting the last 30-minute VWAP for derivatives settlement and changing trading hours from December 7, 2026.
item.dc:creator: Khushboo Tiwari
item.content:encoded: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Thursday announced the much-awaited revisions to the closing auction session (CAS) framework, introducing changes to the settlement methodology, trading timings, and the transition of unexecuted iceberg orders. An iceberg order is a large order split into smaller orders where only a fraction of the total quantity is visible in the order book displayed to the public. The revised framework will take effect from December 7, 2026, except for changes relating to the transition of unexecuted limit and iceberg orders from the continuous trading session (CTS) to CAS, which will come into force from February 8, 2027. Retaining the earlier method, the settlement price of index derivatives will be based on the volume-weighted average prices (VWAP) of constituent securities during the last 30 minutes of the CTS (3.00 pm to 3.30 pm) in the equity cash segment. For expiring stock derivatives, clearing corporations will determine settlement prices using the VWAP of the underlying stock during the last 30 minutes of the CTS across all stock exchanges. Exchanges will provide the VWAP and quantity traded to clearing corporations and continuously disseminate indicative values to market participants in real time during this period. Under the revised timings, CAS will operate as a separate 10-minute session from 3:30 pm to 3:40 pm on all trading days. The order-entry period will close randomly between 3:38 pm and 3:40 pm. Trading in index derivatives will continue until 3:45 pm on regular trading days, but contracts expiring that day will stop trading at 3:30 pm. Trading in stock derivatives will continue until 3:45 pm, including on expiry days. The post-close session in the cash segment will run from 3:50 pm to 4 pm, with trades executed at the closing prices of securities. CAS became effective on August 3 and saw an uproar from the trading community over the settlement price, sharp spikes, and low liquidity. The latest changes were announced following a consultation paper that received over 20,000 suggestions, which was followed by deliberations of the market regulator’s Secondary Market Advisory Committee on Thursday. The regulator had also proposed a blended mechanism, on which several market participants had raised concerns, given the low liquidity in the window. Traders and brokers had favoured the 30-minute VWAP method stating that participants were more familiar with this mechanism and that it was more transparent and operationally well understood. On Thursday, Sebi also specified how unexecuted orders will move from the CTS to CAS. Pending limit orders will generally be carried forward, except stop-loss orders and orders priced beyond the applicable CAS price bands. Unexecuted iceberg orders within the applicable price bands will be converted into fully disclosed limit orders (at fixed/pre-determined price), unless market participants opt out when placing the original orders. These converted orders will have lower time priority than other limit orders carried forward from the continuous session, but higher priority than limit orders placed during CAS. At present, CAS is a 20 minute window from 3:15 pm to 3:35 pm where the reference price calculation and transition from CTS to CAS happens from 3:15 pm to 3:20 pm. In this period, no order entry is allowed. The next five minutes order entry period remains. From 3.25 pm to 3.30 pm, the order entry period is restricted to limit orders only, and no modifications or cancellations of market orders are allowed. In this period, trading closes randomly in the last two minutes. In its consultation paper, Sebi had also proposed prohibiting cancellation of limit orders placed beyond 1 per cent range of the reference price during CAS. However, the regulator skipped this change in the final circular.

item.title: AstraZeneca strikes $40 million AI drug discovery deal with Insitro
item.description: AstraZeneca will pay insitro $40 million upfront to discover AI-driven treatments for liver and heart diseases, with potential milestone payments of up to $1.46 billion ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / News / AstraZeneca strikes $40 million AI drug discovery deal with Insitro

AstraZeneca strikes $40 million AI drug discovery deal with Insitro The multi-year partnership will target severe liver and heart conditions, with insitro eligible for up to $1.46 billion in development and commercial milestone payments

AstraZeneca has partnered with AI biotech firm insitro to discover treatments for severe liver and heart conditions.

Reuters 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 15 2026 | 9:47 PM IST

Listen to This Article

AstraZeneca has teamed up with artificial intelligence biotech company insitro to discover and develop new treatments for difficult to treat liver and heart conditions, the British drugmaker said on Thursday.   Under the agreement, AstraZeneca will pay $40 million up front, with California-based insitro eligible for up to about $1.46 billion in potential development and commercial milestones, as well as a single-digit percentage of future sales in royalties.   The multi-year collaboration will focus on metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a severe liver disease, and cardiomyopathies, a group of diseases that affect the heart muscle. Both have historically lacked effective therapies because researchers have struggled to pinpoint their root biological drivers, the drugmaker said.

Insitro will use its "Virtual Human" AI platform, which combines lab-grown cell models and machine learning, to identify causal disease biology and advance AstraZeneca-nominated targets from discovery to development-candidate stage. AstraZeneca will then run and fund future clinical trials.   The deal builds on insitro's expansion across the pharmaceuticals industry. The biotech company recently expanded its partnership with Bristol Myers Squibb to advance a broader portfolio of targets for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). It also teamed up with Eli Lilly to build AI models that predict pharmacological properties of small molecules â in living organisms.   "Choosing the new targets that we want to put into our discovery pipeline is one of the hardest things we do across research and development," Sharon Barr, executive vice president of biopharmaceuticals R&D at AstraZeneca, told Reuters.

"By the time we read about a new pathway or target (in major scientific journals), it is no longer novel. It's in the public domain and we're already a few steps too late. But when we identify these unique connections early and test them in cellular systems, we're ahead of the game." Barr added that pairing AI tools with experienced scientists allows the company to test fewer molecules in the lab, reduce guesswork and speed the search for effective medicines.     More From This Section

item.title: Google DeepMind ties up with ICRISAT to develop plant genome atlas
item.description: The open-access catalogue will use AI to help breeders identify promising plant combinations faster, while the partnership will also support genome mapping for other crops ...
item.dc:creator: Aashish Aryan
item.content:encoded: Google DeepMind and Google.org have partnered with Hyderabad-headquartered International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT) to launch an open-access global public genetic atlas aimed at identifying the most promising plant combinations, particularly in sorghum, Google India said. “The resulting AI-supported genetic catalogue is aimed at helping breeders and researchers across the world to develop more resilient and productive sorghum varieties faster than traditional methods, which can involve decade-long trial-and-error processes,” the company said in a blog post. Google DeepMind will also support a three-year postdoctoral fellowship at ICRISAT to help develop tools that can map and characterise genomes for other crops and pulses such as chickpea, groundnut and pigeon pea, the company said. “We aim for this collaboration to unlock the global potential of indigenous climate-resilient crops like sorghum, and to empower the agri ecosystem with cutting-edge tools that strengthen global food security and safeguard present and future generations,” Stanford Blade, deputy director general of research and innovation at ICRISAT, said. Separately, Google is expanding access to its Agricultural Understanding Models to enable developers, startups and researchers to build customised solutions for hyperlocal farming challenges and strengthen agricultural resilience, the company said. The move is aimed at widening access to AI tools that can be used to address local agricultural conditions and improve decision-making across the farm ecosystem. Google’s AI Educator Series, first launched in May this year in partnership with five states, is now being expanded to Bihar and Madhya Pradesh. The series will also be made available as a free online resource accessible to users across the country, Google India said. Google.org, Google’s philanthropic arm, will also provide $15 million to The/Nudge to support the growth of micro, small and medium enterprises in India. “This initiative will fund the development of scalable AI tools to expand small enterprises' access to formal credit, market discovery, and compliance,” the company said.

item.title: Would halt chip supply to buyers who develop unsafe AI, says Nvidia CEO
item.description: Jensen Huang said Nvidia would first discuss concerns with an AI developer before considering a supply halt, as the chipmaker pledges $250 million over 5 years to support AI safety research in the UK ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Ian King Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said he would halt the supply of chips to a customer that was developing unsafe AI software, though he doesn’t believe that the current level of concern about the technology is warranted.  “It’s a hypothetical, but yes,” he said in an interview with Bloomberg’s Emily Chang in London when asked if he’d stop supplying an irresponsible developer. “But before you do so, you would have a conversation. We don’t run other people’s companies, and there’s a limit to the judgment we apply to other companies’ use of our technology. Our technology is general-purpose.” Nvidia is the dominant supplier of artificial intelligence accelerators, the chips used to train and run AI models. That’s put it at the center of a debate over whether the software risks growing too powerful and slipping out of human control. AI executives such as Anthropic PBC CEO Dario Amodei have proposed an industrywide slowdown to address the concerns.  Huang, who’s on a tour through Europe ahead of a company event in Berlin, said the fears about AI safety are part of growing pains for an industry expanding quickly. The executive said he believes that the software can be controlled and deployed safely.  As part of its commitment to keeping AI safe, Nvidia is donating $250 million over five years toward UK research into the issue. The support will come in the form of access to time on advanced computers. Various academic institutions in that country, including the University of Oxford and University College London, will study safeguards and ways to control AI agents. “Many of the young companies are going through growing pains, and they’re growing incredibly fast,” Huang said in the interview. “There’s an accountability, responsibility that goes along with building companies that they’re just growing into.” Some of the concern that exists is “self-imposed,” he said, and the industry in general is doing a “horrible job” of explaining the benefits of the new technology. AI itself can be used to safeguard and help contain the technology, Huang added. “We should accelerate the integration of this containment technology into AI systems,” he said. “We should accelerate the development of monitoring technologies, and AI is that monitor. So we should accelerate AI technology.” On a day when Nvidia shares and other chip stocks led declines in US trading, Huang reiterated his belief that AI bubble fears are overdone. Demand for AI infrastructure will continue to outrun the supply of components for years to come, he said. “Eventually supply and demand will harmonize,” he said at an event in London, “but not today.”
